mainEntity.name: How do I read a negative number in two's complement?

acceptedAnswer.text: If the leading bit is 1, the value is negative: flip every bit, add 1, and that gives the binary magnitude — then negate. E.g. in 8 bits, 11111011 flips to 00000100, +1 = 00000101 = 5, so 11111011 represents −5.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between LSR and ASR?

acceptedAnswer.text: LSR (logical shift right) always fills the vacated high bit with 0, treating the value as unsigned. ASR (arithmetic shift right) fills it by copying the sign bit, so a negative two's-complement number stays negative — equivalent to floor division by a power of two.

mainEntity.name: Why does 1111 + 0001 overflow in a 4-bit register?

acceptedAnswer.text: 1111 (15) + 1 = 16 = 10000 in binary, which needs 5 bits. A 4-bit register can't hold it, so the leading 1 is dropped, leaving 0000 and an overflow/carry flag — the same "wraps to zero" behavior real 4-bit hardware shows.

mainEntity.name: Can I enter more bits than the register width?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can, but the value is masked (truncated) to the chosen width before the operation runs, matching what happens when a value doesn't fit in a real register.
